title: APIs and contracts
summary: Design a small book-search API with clear inputs, replies, limits, and errors. Learn why both sides need the same contract.
introduction: A library request slip has boxes for the details the librarian needs. An API is a similar doorway between programs. A clear doorway helps both sides know what to send and what to expect.
learningObjectives: Describe an API contract in plain language
Bound a search reply with a page size
Choose clear replies for empty results and invalid input

blocks.text: An **API**, short for application programming interface, is a way for programs to work together. A **contract** describes the allowed request, the reply, and the meaning of errors.

Our search uses HTTP, the web's request-and-response rules. GET asks to read data. The path names the resource, and query fields after the question mark help choose the results. For this contract, a title match ignores upper- and lower-case letters, so Moon and moon mean the same search text.
A **page** is a small group of results. Returning a page of 20 books is easier to handle than sending a huge catalog at once. A cursor is a marker for where the next page should begin.

Treat a cursor as an opaque value: the client copies it into the next request without taking it apart. The service still checks that it is valid. The sample below is a paper contract, not a live endpoint.

items: Ask for books whose title matches moon, with a limit of 2 records.
Require title to contain 1 to 80 characters after trimming outside spaces.
Allow an integer limit from 1 to 20. If it is omitted, use 10.
Return a list named items and a nextCursor field. Use null when there is no next page.
Use stable IDs so a client does not depend on a book title staying unchanged.

blocks.text: This tiny example uses one shelf location per book. If a title has copies on several shelves, return those locations separately. The full model keeps the shelf on each physical copy, as shown in [Choose the data](/tutorials/system-design/choose-the-data).

blocks.title: APIs and contracts example

blocks.text: Both sides can now be built against the same rules. The page knows where to read the books, how to ask for more, and how to explain an empty result.
Reading a missing individual book, such as GET /v1/books/999, can return 404 Not Found. Searching a collection with no matches is different: the search worked and returned an empty list.
Check input in the service even if the page already checks it. A different client can send a request without using your page. Keep query limits bounded and avoid sending private fields in the reply.

Use a stable order with a tie breaker, such as title followed by book ID, when paging through results. Data may change between pages, so decide whether live changes or a fixed snapshot better fits the task.

Changing a field from number to text can break clients that expect a number. Document changes and keep compatibility rules clear. A version in the path helps name a contract; it does not remove the need to manage changes.

items: A learner sends limit=0. Write the response and explain whether the service should return the whole catalog.
Return 400 with a message such as limit must be from 1 to 20. Do not turn an invalid small limit into an unlimited reply.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not define only the happy reply. Include input limits, empty results, error meanings, and rules for changes to the contract.
